title: Food-centred activity is becoming a social-infrastructure route for connection, belonging, and community participation
source_unit: OECD, Promoting Social Connectedness Through Food
geography: OECD-country and cross-country community food initiatives, including activities to grow, access, prepare, consume, and redistribute food

observations.period: 2026; food and social connectedness as an emerging policy route

denominator.unit: OECD policy and community-initiative evidence frame

policy_priority.value: social connectedness and loneliness have moved steadily up the OECD policy agenda

structural_changes.value: declining in-person socialising, rising solo living, and erosion or transformation of local social infrastructure are identified as concurrent changes

food_route.value: growing, preparing, and eating food with others can provide accessible and adaptable opportunities for connection

priority_groups.value: older people, people living alone, socio-economically disadvantaged people, men, and young people are identified among groups facing elevated or changing disconnection risks

observations.method: OECD synthesis of social-connection evidence, policy strategies, food-centred activities, and community-level implementation experience.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies an emerging policy field and practical pathways; social connectedness outcomes vary by context, program design, participation, and evaluation quality.
observations.subgroup: People experiencing loneliness or isolation, older people, people living alone, socio-economically disadvantaged communities, men, young people, and local food and community organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Food is not inherently socially inclusive; cost, culture, disability, safety, stigma, time, transport, and participation rules can exclude people from food-centred activities.

observations.period: 2026; eight food-based community and government case studies

denominator.unit: in-depth food initiative case studies reviewed by the OECD

activity_stages.value: grow, access, prepare, consume, and redistribute food
activity_stages.unit: food-system activity stages represented in case studies

accessibility.value: food-based activities can be adapted for participation across age, income, culture, and ability

stigma_route.value: purposeful activities such as meals, gardening, and cooking can offer a socially acceptable reason to engage without explicitly framing participation around loneliness

cultural_meaning.value: food can create opportunities for intercultural exchange and connection

observations.method: OECD comparative case-study review of community-led and government-supported food initiatives across multiple countries and food-system stages.
observations.uncertainty: Case studies demonstrate implementation possibilities rather than population-representative effects or universal program success; selection criteria may favor visible or innovative initiatives.
observations.subgroup: Community participants, volunteers, local food organizations, culturally diverse groups, older people, disadvantaged populations, and public agencies supporting food initiatives.
observations.counterinterpretation: Case-study transfer can fail when local food meanings, land access, staffing, food safety, funding, or social norms differ; accessible design requires more than offering food.

observations.period: 2026; food activity and local social-infrastructure renewal

denominator.unit: OECD cross-case social-infrastructure and community-space frame

space_repurposing.value: vacant urban lots, idle farmland, and underused community venues are repurposed into gardens, cafes, dining spaces, and cooking venues

social_infrastructure.value: food initiatives can renew local spaces that facilitate recurring interaction and social capital

co_benefits.value: case studies identify possible co-benefits for nutrition, food security, physical activity, urban greening, biodiversity, soil restoration, and climate resilience

service_bridge.value: community food settings can create routes to other group activities, social services, and support resources

observations.method: OECD case-study synthesis linking food activities to the physical and organizational spaces that support community interaction and broader well-being.
observations.uncertainty: Co-benefits are potential or observed within selected cases, not estimates of average effects; place renewal can also trigger contestation, displacement, or unequal control.
observations.subgroup: Residents, local organizations, land stewards, urban planners, public libraries and community venues, social-service providers, and neighborhoods with underused or neglected spaces.
observations.counterinterpretation: Repurposing space may improve connection only when access is affordable, safe, durable, and governed with local participation; a physical venue alone does not create belonging.

denominator.unit: OECD cross-case implementation and evidence-quality frame

volunteer_dependence.value: many initiatives rely on volunteer resources because of financial constraints

volunteer_risk.value: volunteer dependence can create turnover and burnout risks while also supporting confidence, purpose, and skill development

government_enablers.value: funding, space or land, policy alignment, referral pathways, standards, and monitoring can support development, scaling, and sustainability

evidence_gap.value: existing evidence often relies on qualitative feedback or participant surveys, creating a need for stronger mixed-method evaluation

observations.method: OECD implementation synthesis across community-led and government-supported food initiatives, with explicit attention to organizational resources and evaluation design.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not establish causal effect sizes, cost-effectiveness, or long-term sustainability for the case-study initiatives; implementation conditions differ across places.
observations.subgroup: Volunteers, program staff, community organizations, public agencies, funders, researchers, participants, and social-service partners.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal evaluation can miss cultural meaning and relational value; qualitative evidence remains useful even though it cannot alone establish scale, durability, or causality.

related_sources.claim: OECD's preceding social-connections report provides the comparative loneliness and connection context.
WHO's Commission on Social Connection provides complementary public-health context.

boundary: This record adds a food-culture and social-infrastructure route across connection, belonging, community space, food access, volunteering, public support, and evaluation. It uses aggregate OECD synthesis and selected public case studies, not respondent-level loneliness histories, individual dietary records, household consumption diaries, causal program evaluations, or proof that food initiatives produce the same outcomes in every community.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD report page and full-report executive summary reviewed for policy priority, structural disconnection, eight case studies, food activity stages, accessibility, cultural meaning, space renewal, co-benefits, volunteering, government support, and evidence gaps.
